pages.title: About
pages.content:
ABOUT

About Genba Diary

Genba Diary was founded in 2021 in Rotterdam to replace scattered construction paperwork with one shared daily record. We build software for crews who begin their working day at the site gate.

2021

STORY

Founded on the Site in Rotterdam

Genba Diary B.V. was established in 2021 at Havenkade 41 in Rotterdam. The company was founded by Marta Kowalczyk and Samuel Adeyemi after Marta spent years working as a construction site manager. On every project, Marta kept a bound paper site diary in her cabin, copying handwritten notes from individual foremen at the end of every shift. Samuel joined to build engineering that connects site gates directly to office records. We decided early on that each project should have exactly one diary shared across every crew. When subcontractors maintain separate logs, site managers lose track of deliveries, weather interruptions, and rebar inspections. Today, our Rotterdam team develops software specifically for morning gate briefings, daily trade sign-offs, and clear records that remain intact until project handover.

One diary per site, read by everyone.

Marta Kowalczyk, co-founder

OFFICE

Rotterdam Office and Site Support

Genba Diary operates from Havenkade 41, 3024 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands. Because construction shifts start before typical commercial office hours, our support team is available Monday through Friday from 06:30 to 18:00 CET, and Saturdays from 07:00 to 12:00. We remain closed on Sundays and public holidays. Site managers and project directors can reach our team by calling +31 10 555 0141 or by emailing rollout@genbadiary.example. Every new seven-day pilot begins on a Monday morning with a dedicated gate briefing. Whether your team operates concrete pumps, interior partitions, or roof scaffolding, we make sure support is reachable while your gates are open and morning boards are being marked.

pages.title: Crews
pages.content:
CREWS

Crews

Genba Diary is built for trade crews who gather at the hoist gate each morning and sign off their shift at day's end. Here is how our daily structure supports concrete, fit-out, and roofing operations.

Crews

CREWS

Crews that start the day at a gate.

CREW 01

Concrete & frame

Pour sequences, pump arrivals, rebar checks and cube test logs recorded before the pour begins.

VIEW MORE

CREW 02

Fit-out & finishing

Room-by-room trade handovers, drylining sign-offs, ceiling closures and daily delivery checks.

VIEW MORE

CREW 03

Roofing & façade

Weather thresholds, membrane protection, crane lifts and envelope inspections logged at height.

VIEW MORE

CREW 01

Concrete and Frame Crews

Concrete and structural frame trades face demanding delivery schedules and rigorous quality checks. Foremen start their morning at the gate by checking pump truck access, formwork readiness, and steel reinforcement drawings. With Genba Diary, the concrete foreman photographs rebar placement directly from the mobile app and logs inspection approvals before the pour begins. Ready-mix concrete trucks arriving throughout the day are recorded at the gate with delivery ticket details. When afternoon pours conclude, the crew logs pour volumes, test cube references, and any crane delays. Everything consolidates into the site diary before the 17:00 sign-off, giving the main contractor an indisputable, permanent account of structural progress without anyone chasing paper delivery dockets.

CREW 02

Fit-Out and Finishing Crews

Interior fit-out and finishing contractors coordinate multiple overlapping trades across rooms, corridors, and service shafts. Drywallers, electricians, and joiners require clear documentation of room handovers, dry lining inspections, and completed ceiling closures. Using Genba Diary, finishing foremen photograph partition framing and insulation before wall boards are sealed. Material deliveries through hoist gates are timestamped upon arrival to prevent disputes between subcontractors over shared vertical transport. If predecessor trades delay access to a classroom or corridor, the trade lead logs the delay in the weather and delays section. By completing all six sections before 17:00, interior crews provide project directors with clean visual evidence of completed work and trade clearances.

CREW 03

Roofing and Façade Crews

Roofing and façade teams work in conditions heavily dictated by wind, precipitation, and exterior hoist capacity. Morning boards for envelope trades address high-level safety, harness anchor points, and wind speed thresholds before work begins above ground. In Genba Diary, façade foremen capture panoramic photos of weatherproofing membranes, cladding rail alignments, and perimeter flashings before moving scaffolding. Any sudden rain shower or crane shutdown is logged immediately under weather and delays, creating a verified timeline of standing time. At 17:00, the daily sign-off confirms that open roof sections have been made watertight for the night. The resulting PDF gives clients and engineering consultants full visibility over exterior progress.

NOT YET

Crews Not Yet Suited for Rollout

While Genba Diary supports daylight trade operations across framing, interiors, and envelope packages, certain site operations are not yet suited for our standard pilot rollout. Specifically, night shifts operating underground or in deep basement excavations without cellular or gate connectivity are currently outside our core scope. Our onboarding process requires reliable morning check-in at a physical gate or hoist location where the daily board can be reviewed. Crews that operate without regular gate supervisor contact or on decentralized road maintenance routes should wait for upcoming offline sync modules before scheduling an onboarding briefing. We focus on active multi-crew construction sites where a shared gate routine creates immediate clarity for the whole project team.

pages.title: A diary day
pages.content:
A DIARY DAY

A Diary Day

A complete diary day consists of six simple sections recorded between dawn and dusk. The day closes with a single sign-off at 17:00, creating an unchangeable PDF record for the project file.

17:00

A DIARY DAY

Six sections, one sign-off at 17:00.

Morning board

The foreman photographs the gate briefing board at 06:40, before the 07:00 shift, and confirms it with one tap. The site manager and the office read it at once, and the board is never wiped away.

Crew & hours

Arriving trade foremen check in at the gate before seven. Headcount by trade and the zone each crew works in are recorded, so the main contractor has a register of everyone on site without passing paper rosters around.

Deliveries

The gate guard or materials coordinator logs supplier, material and offloading location when a truck arrives. Ticket numbers and receipt times are entered on the spot and read by the site manager that afternoon.

Photos & marks

Supervisors take timestamped photos with marks, such as rebar spacing or concealed services before dry lining. Anyone on the project can read them the same day, and nothing has to be reconstructed from memory.

Weather & delays

Rain, high gusts, hoist stoppages and outages are recorded when they happen by the crew affected. The delay is on the record by 17:00, so nobody has to argue later why a lift was suspended.

Sign-off

At 17:00 the site manager reviews all six sections in the cabin and signs off on the screen. Genba Diary then locks the day into one daily PDF that goes to the office and the handover file.

MORNING

Morning Board and Crew Hours

Every diary day begins at 06:40 at the hoist gate. The site manager or lead foreman reviews the morning whiteboard, checking shift objectives, crane allocation, and safety precautions. Instead of retyping the board into a complex software form, the foreman takes a high-resolution photograph of the physical gate board and confirms it with a single tap. Before the 07:00 shift begins, arriving trade foremen check in at the gate. The crew and hours section captures worker headcounts by trade and logs assigned zones across the site. By 07:00, the main contractor has an accurate register of every worker on site without passing paper rosters around the hoists.

DURING THE SHIFT

Deliveries, Photos, and Weather Delays

As work unfolds during the shift, three dynamic sections capture site events as they occur. When delivery flatbeds arrive, the gate guard or materials coordinator logs the supplier, material type, and offloading location under Deliveries. Throughout the day, supervisors take timestamped site photos with marked annotations under Photos & marks, recording structural steel connections, rebar spacing, and concealed plumbing before dry lining. If conditions turn severe, the Weather & delays section records rain volume, high wind gusts, hoist stoppages, or utility outages. Because entries are logged in real time at the gate or on deck, project managers avoid retrospective arguments regarding why crane lifts were suspended or deliveries delayed.

SIGN-OFF

Daily Sign-Off at 17:00

At 17:00, the site manager sits down in the site office or cabin to review the day's record. All six sections—Morning board, Crew & hours, Deliveries, Photos & marks, Weather & delays, and Sign-off—are compiled into a clear, unified view. The site manager reviews subcontractor entries, checks that all trades have completed their logs, and signs off digitally on the screen. Once signed at 17:00, Genba Diary generates an unalterable daily PDF report. This document is automatically archived and emailed to designated project stakeholders and the main contractor's office, ensuring that the day's facts are locked, transparent, and ready for the final handover file.

SAMPLE DAY

Sample Site Schedule

One standard day follows six checkpoints across the site, and every crew works to the same rhythm.

06:40

Morning board photographed at Gate 2.

07:00

Crew arrivals and worker hours confirmed for every active trade.

10:30

Morning deliveries and pallet receipts logged at the hoist entrance.

14:00

Inspection photos, rebar marks and trade progress notes uploaded.

16:30

Weather readings, wind delays and equipment issues entered.

17:00

Site manager signs off and exports the daily PDF summary.

pages.title: Rollout
pages.content:
ROLLOUT

Rollout

We introduce Genba Diary to your project through a structured seven-day pilot for one site and one crew. The rollout requires no software installation fees and is completely free of charge.

7 days

FOUR STAGES

The Four-Stage Rollout Schedule

Our seven-day pilot follows four clear stages tested across busy construction sites. Day 1 begins with a request form followed by a 30-minute call with rollout lead Inès Laurent to confirm site parameters and trade schedules. On Day 2, rollout specialist Jonas Brandt conducts a 45-minute gate briefing at your hoist gate before the 07:00 shift begins, adding the crew to the diary. During Days 3 to 6, the crew completes the six daily sections while Jonas reads the entries every afternoon by 18:00 and leaves one helpful note. On Day 7, the site manager and rollout lead hold a one-hour review to evaluate the diary, examine generated PDFs, and decide whether to keep, extend, or stop the setup.

Day 1

Request and call

Submit the request form and complete a focused 30-minute call with the rollout lead.

Day 2

Gate briefing

A 45-minute briefing at the hoist gate before the 07:00 shift adds the crew to the diary.

Days 3–6

Diary days

The crew writes the six daily sections; our rollout specialist reads each day by 18:00 and leaves one note.

Day 7

Review

One hour with the site manager to keep, extend or stop. Nothing is billed for the pilot.

YOUR SITE

What We Need from Your Site

Starting a pilot requires minimal preparation from the site team. We ask for three practical commitments prior to Day 2. First, your site must provide adequate cellular signal at the hoist gate or entrance cabin so photos and check-ins upload smoothly. Second, each participating crew must have access to at least one smartphone or tablet with an operational camera. Third, the site manager and participating trade foremen must allocate 45 minutes before the 07:00 morning shift for Jonas Brandt's gate briefing. We do not require specialized hardware installations or IT integration. Because the pilot is completely free, your team can evaluate the system under real field conditions without commercial commitment.

AFTER DAY 7

Next Steps After Day 7

At the conclusion of the Day 7 review, site management chooses how to proceed. If your team decides to stop, the pilot concludes immediately and nothing is billed. You retain all generated daily PDFs from the trial week for your site records. If you decide to continue, you can transition directly to our Site plan at $59 per site per month with unlimited crew members, or expand across multiple projects with our Office plan at $390 per month for up to 10 active sites. You can also book an on-site onboarding day for $480 to brief up to 3 additional crews. Every pilot starts on a Monday morning, so request a rollout today to reserve your upcoming slot.

pages.title: Plans
pages.content:
PLANS

Plans

Genba Diary offers transparent pricing in US dollars with no setup fees or long-term lock-in. Start with our seven-day free pilot and scale across your active sites as needed.

$0
pilot

PLANS

Plans and Pricing Overview

We provide straightforward pricing options designed for individual site managers and multi-project construction companies. Our Pilot rollout costs $0 and includes one site, one crew, seven days of full access, and an on-site gate briefing.

Prices exclude VAT. Monthly plans can be cancelled at the end of any billing month.

BILLING

Billing Terms and Site Management

All Genba Diary plans are billed monthly in US dollars without currency conversion markups or hidden administration charges. Subscription fees are calculated solely on active sites where daily entries and logs are being recorded. When a construction project finishes, you can mark the site as closed at the end of the current billing month to stop recurring subscription fees. There are no mandatory annual contracts, and you can cancel any site subscription at month end directly from the account portal. Support is always included for active subscribers during our standard hours from Monday to Friday 06:30 to 18:00 CET and Saturday 07:00 to 12:00, ensuring your site personnel receive rapid technical assistance whenever required.

QUESTIONS

Billing questions

How does monthly billing work across active sites?

Billing is calculated on a per-site basis each month. If you subscribe to the Site plan at $59 per site per month, you pay only for projects currently under active construction. If your company manages multiple concurrent projects, upgrading to the Office plan at $390 per month covers up to 10 active sites under a single consolidated invoice. Subcontractor trade foremen and site operatives can be added with unlimited accounts without incurring per-user charges. You can activate or deactivate sites at any time, and billing adjustments take effect at the conclusion of the monthly billing cycle.

What is billed if we stop after the pilot rollout?

Nothing is billed if you decide to stop using Genba Diary at the end of the seven-day pilot. The pilot rollout is provided at $0 with no credit card required at registration. During the trial week, your site team receives full access to the six daily diary sections, gate briefing from Jonas Brandt, and daily reviews by our rollout specialists. If you determine during the Day 7 review that the app does not match your current field routine, your account closes without invoice or penalty. All PDF records created during the seven trial days remain yours to keep.

How is archive export charged when a site closes?

When a project reaches practical completion and daily work stops, you can order an Archive export for $35 per site. This one-off service compiles the entire historical record of the project into a comprehensive package. It includes all signed daily PDFs from inception to completion, high-resolution original site photos, delivery logs, and weather records structured for the client handover file. Once exported, the site is closed in your subscription portal so no ongoing monthly charges accrue. If your project generated extensive documentation exceeding standard limits, extra photo storage of +100 GB can be maintained for $15 per month until final archive download.

Request a rollout

WAITLIST

Waitlist

Join the early-access waitlist for our upcoming Handover Pack module. Reserve your place to streamline project closeout and export complete digital records directly to client handover files.

Early

Early Access to the Handover Pack Module

Genba Diary is currently developing the Handover Pack module to assemble this documentation automatically as work proceeds. By connecting daily sign-offs, photo inspection marks, and gate delivery registers into a unified archive, the module produces a structured handover bundle compliant with engineering handover requirements. Early waitlist participants will test the module on active projects before general release, gaining early access to automated PDF indexing and export tools designed by Tomás Ortega and Samuel Adeyemi.

SIGN UP

To register your interest in the Handover Pack early-access programme, submit your contact name, work email address, company name, and typical crew size through our waitlist form. Priority onboarding is given to general contractors and trade specialists currently running active sites with multiple subcontractor crews. Once your site profile is reviewed, rollout lead Inès Laurent will contact your team to discuss project completion dates and handover milestones. There is no software charge for participating in the early-access programme during the trial phase. We invite active site managers to help refine the export features that turn everyday gate records into an organized handover file.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
PRIVACY

Privacy Policy

Genba Diary B.V. respects your privacy and handles all construction records and personal contact information with care. This policy outlines how we collect, store, and protect project data.

Collection and Processing of Site Data

Genba Diary B.V., located at Havenkade 41, 3024 AB Rotterdam, Netherlands, operates as the data controller for account contact details and the data processor for site diary content. We collect information necessary to operate our service, including site manager names, phone numbers, trade classifications, and email addresses. During daily operations, the application records uploaded photographs of morning boards, worker headcounts, gate delivery records, and signed daily PDFs. All operational site data is gathered exclusively to maintain your project diary and provide customer support between 06:30 and 18:00 CET. We do not sell site data, license contractor records to third parties, or use uploaded site photos for automated marketing.

Data Retention and Archive Export

Site diary entries, inspection marks, and daily PDFs remain stored securely throughout the duration of your active subscription. When a project concludes and the subscription is closed at month end, project data is retained for a standard transition period to permit archive export. Customers who purchase our Archive export for $35 per site receive a full export of signed daily PDFs and high-resolution photo records for their handover file. Accounts requiring extended cloud hosting can maintain extra photo storage of +100 GB for $15 per month. You may request data deletion or inquire about our privacy practices by contacting our privacy officer at rollout@genbadiary.example or calling +31 10 555 0141.

posts.title: The board that is no longer wiped
posts.excerpt: Site manager Lena Hoffmann explains how four concrete crews on a six-storey housing block replaced disappearing whiteboard notes with a permanent daily record.
posts.content:
At six-thirty every morning on the Harbourline Construction site, four concrete crews gather around the hoist gate. The project is a six-storey housing block with a reinforced concrete frame, where daily progress depends entirely on pump coordination, crane availability, and timely rebar inspections. For two years, site manager Lena Hoffmann managed that routine with a dry-wipe marker on an enamel whiteboard mounted to the gate hoarding. By five in the afternoon, after concrete wagons had departed and shift handovers were completed, someone inevitably wiped the board clean with a rag to prepare for the following morning. The shift was finished, but the operational history of the day vanished with it.

When disputed delivery times arose or engineering consultants requested proof of pre-pour inspections, Lena had to rely on memory or dig through crumpled paper dockets collected from truck drivers. Subcontractors kept their own private notes in pocket notebooks, but the main contractor had no unified record. Harbourline Construction decided to pilot Genba Diary on the housing block, beginning with a seven-day trial for one concrete crew. The rollout started on a Monday morning following a gate briefing conducted by Jonas Brandt before the 07:00 shift.

The transformation in site routine was immediate and practical. The morning whiteboard remained in place at Gate 2, but at 06:40 the foreman photographed the completed board directly into the app instead of retyping shift assignments into a complex database. Arriving workers checked in by trade before seven, logging crew headcounts across the slab. When concrete delivery trucks arrived at the gate, the gateman entered delivery ticket numbers, mix designations, and arrival times on a tablet. Foremen took timestamped photos of rebar ties and formwork joints before pump hoses began discharging concrete.

If a pump line clogged or high winds halted the tower crane, foremen recorded the downtime under the weather and delays section rather than leaving it to afternoon debate. At 17:00, Lena sat down in the site office to review the six completed sections. With all four crews contributing to the same site diary, Lena signed off the day digitally. The platform generated a complete daily PDF summary that locked the day's events into the project archive and emailed a copy to the engineering team.

The board used to be wiped at five. Now the day stays.

Lena Hoffmann, site manager

When the seven-day pilot ended, Harbourline Construction transitioned the housing block to the regular Site plan at $59 per site per month. The concrete frame has progressed level by level with every pour, delivery, and inspection cleanly documented. Instead of hunting down missing paperwork during project audits, the site team has an unchangeable daily log that proves exactly what happened on site from gate opening to final sign-off.

Having a single diary shared across all four crews removed the daily friction between subcontractors and the main contractor. Nobody had to learn an overwhelming software suite or spend hours typing reports after a hard shift on the frame. The routine stayed rooted at the gate, where the work actually happens. For Lena and her team, capturing the morning board and signing off at 17:00 has become as fundamental to pouring concrete as checking the slump test or wearing a white helmet.

posts.title: Handovers, room by room
posts.excerpt: Moreau Interiors records ceiling closures and drylining inspections per room.
posts.content:
Karim Benali is a foreman on the fit-out of a school refurbishment with two crews at Moreau Interiors. Each room has its own entry in the diary.

Ceiling closures and drylining inspections are recorded as they happen, so handovers between joiners and decorators do not wait for a late sign-off.

posts.content:
Ruth Okonkwo leads the roof and façade of a logistics hall with three crews at Northfield Roofing. Wind limits, crane lifts and membrane checks are written and photographed where they happen.

posts.title: Why the board is a photo, not a form
posts.excerpt: The morning board is a photograph, because a gate briefing is a thing you look at.
posts.content:
The first section of every diary day is a photograph of the gate briefing board. A form would ask the foreman to type what the board already says.

A photo takes seconds, cannot be mistyped and shows the same thing to the office that the crew saw at the gate.

posts.title: Writing a diary day offline
posts.excerpt: The diary works without signal and syncs when it returns.
posts.content:
Signal at a hoist gate comes and goes. The diary stores every entry on the device and syncs it automatically once signal returns.

Rain notes, photos and the 17:00 sign-off can all be written offline.
